first.rationale: The two observed declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are upstream funnel problems, and the inherited record most directly addresses them: memory_86 (shorter onboarding lifts completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer required signup fields lifts first-week activation), with memory_91 as a related but narrower lever. Promotional pricing is the emotionally salient response to the competitor, but memory_73 is explicitly caveated aafter pooled after a mid-test redefinition, so its measured lift is not trustworthy at face value, and discounting into a price war trades near-term acquisition against the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Referral incentives (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) address neither of the two live regressions this week. I am spending verification on memory_86 because it is the primary basis for my intended action and I do not want to build on an unexamined claim, and on memory_73 because it is the strongest competing option and its known defect determines whether it should be reconsidered at all. Downstream value risk is real in both directions: cutting signup fields can raise activation while degrading lead qualification data and downstream pipeline quality (a tension with memory_44's finding that qualified paths convert better), so the experiment must measure qualified-revenue-per-signup and not just completion/activation rates. Uncertainty preserved: the inherited findings are from days 12-61 under different competitive conditions, and the current declines may be driven by competitor-induced mix shift rather than funnel friction, in which case a funnel fix will underperform its historical effect size. If verification shows memory_86's lift was measured only on a cohort unlike today's, or shows memory_73's pooling defect was benign and the pricing effect held, I will revisit before committing. Standard experiment scale with a clean control, not a broad rollout.
